items.title: Roy Haynes — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: It was Joe Benjamin at first and John Malachi.

ctx.x: It was Joe Benjamin at first and John Malachi. Then Jimmy Jones had come back, because he was sick for a while. Then when he left, I think Ronnell Bright. Then Joe had an automobile accident. I think Richard Davis had come in. Then when Ronnell Bright came in, it started changing, going in another . . .
So that period, from basically – from ’54 to ’58 – is that? – it was late ’52? When did you . . .?

items.title: 68089_John Malachi oral history interview
items.q: Roy Haynes is a drummer that just turned out to be one of my favorite drummers that I have worked with.

ctx.x: And then we came back to the United States, New York. When we came back, we had a few days rest, and it was time to hit the road again in the good old United States, and started hitting the clubs. But before we left New York, they had to get a trio together, which came up again. At that particular time, Israel Crosby I think was working with Benny Goodman, he'd gone on tour or something with Benny Goodman. Of course, Bruz had gone to California; I don't know what was happening. But we got Roy Haynes, the drummer…

Both are very fine musicians. Roy Haynes is a drummer that just turned out to be one of my favorite drummers that I have worked with. I think in a big band situation, Shadow Wilson was always my favorite, and of course, Art Blakey -- depending on the style that the band was playing. In a combo situation, and especially when it came to accompanying a singer, I think Roy Haynes is just about the greatest that I've ever worked with. First of all, we used to kid him a lot -- he's a frustrated singer himself. That's…
